title: "GAMP 5 and the V-Model"

## The question this course exists to answer

Last spring, a validation package closed with one question left hanging. Lakeshore ran twelve
targeted tests against an operating-system patch, declared no impact to BECS's (Blood
Establishment Computer Software's) validated state, and both required signatures landed. Nobody
in that review could say whether twelve was actually the right number, or just a number that
felt defensible at the time. This course exists to give you a real way to answer that question —
not by revisiting that patch today, but by building, from the ground up, the method a real
answer would require.

That method starts somewhere else entirely: a new project, with its own draft plan, already
making the same kind of judgment call before a single test runs.

A few months after that patch closed out, Lakeshore's BECS vendor announced end-of-support for
the release running today. No more security patches, no more support tickets, on a clock
Lakeshore doesn't control. The only real option is to move to the vendor's new major release —
call it Release B. That upgrade is now a project, with a validation package number of its own:
**VAL-1203**, distinct from everything this curriculum has already named (VIA-0842, DEV-1147,
CAPA-1147-A, VRA-0219). Scope: the central BECS application server, plus the BECS clients running
at both of Lakeshore's satellite collection sites, Brookfield and Fairview. One more piece of
scope matters a lot, for reasons that will come back twice more later in this course: a small
piece of software Lakeshore IT itself wrote and maintains, a translation script that takes result
messages out of the testing lab's LIS (laboratory information system — the software the testing
lab runs its own workflows on) and reformats them into what BECS expects on the way in. Nobody
sells that script. Nobody else has ever tested it. It's Lakeshore's.

The draft validation plan and risk assessment for VAL-1203 reach your desk for review. They were
written by the **Quality Validation Lead** — the role that signs test-scope rationales, the one
your Quality Analyst already knows to route sufficiency questions to — working with IT and the
vendor's implementation consultant. Quality's sign-off is blocking, same as always. You're the
system-owner co-approver, same as always.

Your systems administrator has already read it, and he's got a position: "It's a Category 4
vendor product. The vendor built it, the vendor tested it before they ever shipped it to us. We
run a smoke test, confirm it installed, and we're done."

Attached to the plan is a first draft of the URS (user requirements specification — the document
that states, in plain business language, what the system has to do). Three rows are worth
sitting with before you read any further:

| Req ID | Requirement | Risk ranking |
|---|---|---|
| REQ-014 | "The system shall be user-friendly for all BECS users." | — |
| REQ-022 | "The system shall not permit release of a blood component until all required test results for that donation are recorded as complete." | *(blank)* |
| *(none)* | *(no requirement covers the LIS-to-BECS results translation script at all)* | — |

Something is wrong with the sysadmin's one-liner, and with all three rows on that table. By the
end of this lesson you'll be able to say exactly what, and why a category label was never going
to settle it either way.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure mode a validation plan like VAL-1203's is actually built to prevent: software
that silently does less than it's supposed to do, or more than it should, on a system that stands
between a unit of blood and the patient who receives it. Nobody ships code that's supposed to
fail. Every defect that ever reached production, in any industry, passed through someone who
believed the software did what they thought it did. Validation is the discipline of not taking
that belief on faith — proving, with evidence someone else can check later, that the system
actually does what you need it to do, before you let it decide anything that matters.

You already own the ITSM (IT service management) vocabulary for the shape of this problem, even
though you've never had to apply it to a question this strict.

**SDLC (software development lifecycle) and release management** already structure how you move
any system from requirements to a live release: gather requirements, design, build, test, deploy.
Nothing about that shape is new here. What's new is how much proof has to exist at each step
before you're allowed to move on, and who's allowed to sign off on "good enough."

**Requirements engineering** is a discipline you already practice, even if nobody at Lakeshore
calls it that: a requirement that can't be tested isn't a requirement, it's a wish. You already
know a bad user story when you see one in a sprint backlog. The standard here is the same
instinct, with less room for charity.

**CI (configuration item) classification by type** is the cleanest bridge of all. Your CMDB
(configuration management database) already sorts systems by what kind of thing they are —
infrastructure, commercial package, custom application — because that classification drives which
change model applies by default: a routine patch to a commodity server gets a lighter touch than
a change to bespoke code nobody else runs. GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice) — an
industry framework from ISPE (the International Society for Pharmaceutical Engineering), now in
its Second Edition, published July 2022, and one you should treat as **industry practice, not
FDA regulation** anywhere you encounter it — does the same sorting, for the same reason: knowing
what *kind* of software a thing is tells you the default amount of scrutiny it should get.

Here's where the regulated world demands more than your CMDB's default logic does. In ordinary IT
risk scoring, a component with a long, quiet track record earns a lower assumed likelihood of
failure over time — that's usually reasonable. FDA's BECS guidance (FDA's current, non-binding
recommendations on this topic — more on that tier distinction below) says the opposite for
software performing a function like this: because software defects are hard to predict and hard
to see coming, you should **assume most hazards are likely, not unlikely**, until a documented
risk assessment says otherwise. A GAMP category sets where you start. A documented risk
assessment — not the category, and not a vendor's reputation — is what's allowed to say where you
actually need to end up.

## The rule in plain English

Two separate things are happening inside VAL-1203's draft plan, and your sysadmin has only
noticed one of them.

**First: every piece of software in the BECS upgrade sorts into one of four GAMP categories**,
industry practice's own names for "what kind of thing is this." No Category 2 — it fell out of
use industry-wide and nobody uses it anymore.

- **Category 1 — infrastructure.** The operating system and the database engine underneath BECS.
  Nobody configured business logic into it; it's the platform everything else runs on. Lowest
  default scrutiny, because its behavior isn't specific to Lakeshore's use of it.
- **Category 3 — non-configured product.** Software used exactly as the vendor ships it, with no
  configuration choices that change its behavior. Not much of VAL-1203's stack lives here, but
  it's the category a vendor tool earns when Lakeshore runs it untouched, out of the box.
- **Category 4 — configured product.** BECS itself, as Lakeshore configures it: the vendor built
  the product, but Lakeshore's own configuration choices — business rules, user roles, interface
  mappings, report layouts — shape how it actually behaves at Lakeshore. That configuration is
  Lakeshore's own work, and it needs to be validated as Lakeshore built it, not just as the vendor
  shipped it.
- **Category 5 — custom/bespoke.** Code nobody but Lakeshore wrote. The LIS-to-BECS translation
  script lives here. Nothing about it was vendor-tested, vendor-documented, or vendor-supported,
  because it isn't the vendor's code.

What a category implies is a *starting point* for how much validation effort a thing probably
needs — infrastructure usually needs less than bespoke code, because bespoke code is the one
category where nobody besides Lakeshore has ever looked at it. That's useful. It's also where
your sysadmin stopped reading.

**Second: a documented risk assessment, not the category, is what actually sets test depth.**
ISPE's own description of GAMP 5's Second Edition is worth knowing here, in its own words,
paraphrased rather than quoted (it's a paid publication, so treat this as a pointer, not a
source to cite from): the Second Edition leans harder than the first toward **critical thinking**
by people who actually understand the system, instead of mechanically running every Category 4
system through the same fixed test recipe. A category tells you where to start looking. It was
never built to tell you where to stop.

That's exactly the gap in your sysadmin's "Category 4, vendor tested it, smoke test's enough"
position. BECS *as Lakeshore configures it* is Category 4 — true. But Category 4 covers
everything from a report template nobody relies on to a configuration setting that gates whether
a unit of blood gets released. Those two don't deserve the same test depth just because they
share a category number. What decides test depth is risk: how bad is it if this breaks, and how
likely is it that nobody would notice before it mattered. A category sorts software. A risk
assessment sizes the response.

### The V-model: specs going down, tests going up

Here's the shape every validation plan in this course will keep coming back to, industry
practice's own way of drawing the relationship between what you ask for and what you prove.
Picture a capital V. Down the left side, you write what the system is supposed to do, at three
levels of increasing detail:

- **URS (user requirements specification)** — what Lakeshore, as the business, needs the system to
  do. Plain language, no implementation detail.
- **FS or FRS (functional specification / functional requirements specification)** — how the
  system will actually behave to satisfy each URS requirement. Still no code-level detail, but
  specific enough that someone could build to it.
- **DS (design specification)** — the technical design: the exact configuration setting, workflow
  rule, or code logic that implements each functional requirement.

Up the right side, each level gets a test that answers it, industry practice's common pairing,
named here as a concept only — you'll meet each test type's actual contents in the next module:

- **DS pairs with IQ** (installation qualification) — does the system exist, installed and
  configured, as the design specification says it should?
- **FS pairs with OQ** (operational qualification) — does each function actually work the way the
  functional spec says it should?
- **URS pairs with PQ** (performance qualification) — does the system, running at Lakeshore, with
  Lakeshore's own people and procedures, actually meet the business need the URS stated?

That's the whole shape: every requirement you write down on the way down the V gets a test that
answers it on the way up. A requirement with no test is a promise nobody checked. A test with no
requirement behind it is effort spent proving nothing anyone asked for.

**What makes a URS/FRS/DS requirement good or bad is whether it can fail.** Look again at
VAL-1203's draft rows. REQ-014 — "the system shall be user-friendly" — cannot fail. Nobody can
write a test case with a pass/fail outcome against it, because nothing in it says what
"user-friendly" means in a way two reviewers would agree on. It's not a requirement — it's a
wish wearing a requirement's row number. A good version of that same intent is testable:
something like "a user can complete donor check-in in under three steps from the main screen."

REQ-022 — the release-gate requirement — is the opposite problem. The *wording* is genuinely
testable. What's missing is the risk ranking next to it, and that's not a formatting gap. This
is the requirement that gates whether an incompletely-tested unit of blood can be released.
Leave its risk ranking blank, and nothing tells the person building the test plan that this row
deserves more scrutiny than a report-formatting preference three rows below it. A risk ranking
isn't decoration on a URS row. It's the input the rest of the V depends on.

And the row that doesn't exist at all — nothing in the draft URS covers the LIS-to-BECS
translation script — is the sharpest gap of the three. That script is Category 5: the one
category where nobody but Lakeshore has ever tested it. A URS with no row for it means nobody has
even started the V for the one component with the least outside scrutiny behind it already.

### The vendor's V, and Lakeshore's V

One more distinction, worth holding onto in two sentences, because the next two modules will
build real weight on top of it. The vendor ran its own V — its own internal build-and-test
process — before Release B ever shipped to a customer; that's the vendor's own validation,
module 4's subject, not something Lakeshore performs or can substitute for its own. VAL-1203 is
**Lakeshore's** V: proving, in Lakeshore's own facility, with Lakeshore's own configuration, data,
and people, that the system meets Lakeshore's requirements — the subject module 3 picks up when
it asks what a vendor's clearance can and can't tell you about the version you actually run.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 211.68(a) | "Two-eleven point sixty-eight, paragraph a" | Automated, mechanical, or electronic equipment — including computers — used in manufacturing must be routinely calibrated, inspected, or checked under a written program designed to assure proper performance, with written records of those checks maintained. | The regulatory floor VAL-1203's validation plan exists to satisfy — the reason a written, controlled validation plan isn't optional paperwork, it's what the regulation itself requires before routine use. |
| 21 CFR 210.2(a) | "Two-ten point two, paragraph a" | Part 211 (drug CGMP, current good manufacturing practice) and Parts 600–680 (biological products, including blood) "supplement, not supersede, each other." | The reason a regulation written for drug manufacturing — 211.68 — reaches a blood establishment's computer system at all. |

## The actual text

The validation floor, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/211.68.md`:

> (a) Automatic, mechanical, or electronic equipment or other types of equipment, including
> computers, or related systems that will perform a function satisfactorily, may be used in the
> manufacture, processing, packing, and holding of a drug product. If such equipment is so used,
> it shall be routinely calibrated, inspected, or checked according to a written program designed
> to assure proper performance. Written records of those calibration checks and inspections shall
> be maintained.

Read that as the bar VAL-1203's validation plan has to clear: a written program, routine checks,
and records someone can produce later. Nothing in that sentence mentions GAMP, categories,
IQ/OQ/PQ, or a V-model — because none of that vocabulary is regulatory. It's industry's own
answer to "how do I satisfy this sentence in a way I can defend."

The supplementation sentence, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/210.2.md`:

> The regulations in this part and in parts 211, 213, 225, and 226 of this chapter as they may
> pertain to a drug; in parts 600 through 680 of this chapter as they may pertain to a biological
> product for human use; ... shall be considered to supplement, not supersede, each other, unless
> the regulations explicitly provide otherwise.

Blood is regulated under Parts 600–680, not Part 211. 210.2(a) is the clause that keeps a
drug-manufacturing section like 211.68 from simply not applying to a blood establishment: the two
sets of regulations layer on top of each other instead of one replacing the other. That's why
FDA's own BECS guidance can say, without contradiction, that 211.68 is one of the requirements
that reaches Lakeshore's computer systems.

And FDA's BECS guidance says exactly that, in its own introduction, quoted from
`sources/fda-guidance/becs-validation-users-facility-2013.md` — labeled here as guidance, because
that's what it is, not binding regulation:

> This guidance describes the following: • Requirements in Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations
> (21 CFR) (e.g., 21 CFR 211.68, 606.100(b), and 606.160) that apply to blood establishment
> validation of systems; and • FDA's recommendations for the validation of systems.

That sentence is the guidance naming its own two tiers side by side: things it's quoting out of
actual regulation (211.68, 606.100(b), 606.160), and everything else, which is FDA's
recommendation. The guidance is careful about this distinction everywhere, including stating its
own rule for reading it:

> The use of the word should in FDA guidances means that something is suggested or recommended,
> but not required.

Keep that "shall versus should" test running under everything else in this lesson. When the
guidance says a validation plan "must" require validation before routine use, it's citing
211.68(a) — regulation. When it recommends testing "worst case scenarios" or keeping a remote
access log, that's FDA's current thinking, worth doing, not independently enforceable.

Two more guidance-tier sentences are worth having in front of you, both doing real work in this
lesson. On how much confidence is enough:

> Generally, software validation is a matter of developing a "level of confidence" (Ref. 1) that
> the software device meets all requirements and user expectations for the automated functions
> and features of the software.

And on how to assume probability when you can't actually measure it:

> Because of the complexity of software, especially BECS, it is difficult to predict the
> probability of a hazard occurrence. Therefore, when you conduct your risk assessment, we
> recommend you consider most hazards to have a high probability of occurrence.

That second sentence is the guidance-tier twist behind this lesson's likelihood-severity-
detectability vocabulary from `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`: for BECS, don't let a plausible-
sounding "this probably won't happen" lower your risk ranking on its own. Let severity and
detectability carry the weight instead, and make likelihood do less work than it normally would.

One more citation earns a name here and nothing more: **21 CFR 11.10(a)**, the Part 11
(electronic records and signatures) clause earlier modules already quoted for "consistent
intended performance." It isn't the hook doing the work in this lesson — 211.68(a) is — and
exactly why that's true is the Part 11 hook module 5 will unpack. Leave it there for now.

AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSE) framework — the ten-part structure behind an AABB
accreditation assessment, introduced earlier in this curriculum — sits on top of all of this,
paraphrased only, no standard number: validation work like VAL-1203 lives under **QSE 5, Process
Control**, the theme covering how a blood establishment controls and proves out a regulated
process, software included.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reading VAL-1203's file isn't going to ask whether the
upgrade is "Category 4." They're going to ask for the document that shows Lakeshore actually
reasoned through the risk, not just filed a category label and moved on. Three things, in order:

**A documented risk assessment, performed before the test plan was written, not after.** Not a
sentence buried in a validation plan's introduction that says "this is a Category 4 system, so
standard testing applies." A real assessment: which functions were evaluated, what hazard each
one could cause if it failed, and why the resulting test depth follows from that, not from a
category number alone.

**A URS where every requirement touching a critical function carries an explicit risk ranking.**
Not every row needs the same ranking — a report-formatting preference and a release gate
shouldn't carry equal weight — but every row needs *some* ranking, set before testing starts, not
reverse-engineered afterward to match whatever got tested.

**Evidence the in-house component got its own full treatment**, not a free ride on BECS's
Category 4 status. A translation script Lakeshore wrote doesn't inherit anyone else's testing.
If the URS has no row for it, that's the gap an inspector finds in about thirty seconds — because
it's the one piece of this upgrade nobody outside Lakeshore has ever put a test case against.

A bad answer to "why wasn't this requirement risk-ranked" sounds like "it's a Category 4 vendor
system, we trusted their testing." A good answer points to a dated risk assessment, signed by
someone qualified to make that call, with the reasoning written down.

## Common traps

**"It's a Category 4 vendor product, so the vendor's testing covers it."** This is your
sysadmin's exact position, and it's the single most common misreading of GAMP categories in the
industry. A category describes what *kind* of software something is. It doesn't describe how much
risk it carries at this specific site, in this specific configuration, for this specific function.
FDA's guidance is blunt about who owns the result regardless of category: equipment vendors and
consultants "may provide assistance," but "you are ultimately responsible for validation of your
system in your facility." The vendor tested its own product, in its own environment, against its
own intended uses. That's an input to Lakeshore's validation. It was never a substitute for it.

**"The category tells you the test depth, so once you know it's Category 4, you know how hard to
test."** Backwards. The category sets a default starting point — useful for staffing and planning
a validation project, the same way knowing a CI's type helps you pick a default change model. What
actually sets depth is the risk assessment: which functions are high-consequence, how likely a
hazard really is (assume likely, per the guidance, not unlikely), and how bad it is if nobody
catches a failure before it reaches a patient. Two Category 4 systems can reasonably get very
different test depths, and a validation plan that doesn't show why is missing its real argument.

## What this means for your job

- **When a GAMP category and a risk assessment point to different test depths, trust the risk
  assessment.** A category is a starting assumption; a documented, signed risk assessment is a
  decision. If VAL-1203's plan leans on "it's Category 4" instead of a risk assessment, send it
  back before you co-sign.
- **Ask whether the risk assessment assumed each hazard is likely or unlikely, and why.** FDA's
  guidance recommends assuming most software hazards have a high probability of occurrence. A
  risk assessment that quietly assumes low probability with no stated reason is worth a direct
  question.
- **Read every URS row for whether it could actually fail a test.** "User-friendly," "intuitive,"
  "should work correctly" — none of these can fail, so nothing written against them can pass or
  fail either. Send vague rows back before they reach a functional spec.
- **Check that every critical-function requirement carries a risk ranking before testing starts**,
  not after someone notices a gap later. A blank ranking next to a release gate means nobody has
  yet decided how hard that row needs to be tested.
- **Treat every in-house-built piece as its own full V, with no inherited credit from BECS's
  Category 4 status.** If a script, report, or interface Lakeshore itself wrote isn't in the URS
  with its own requirements, risk ranking, and eventual test evidence, nobody has started
  validating it at all.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Someone on the upgrade project says, "FDA's 2026 Computer Software Assurance guidance replaced computer system validation, so we can drop scripted testing on BECS." Accurate?

No, on two separate grounds. First, that guidance (`sources/fda-guidance/csa-production-qms-software-2026-excerpt.md`) covers computer software used in a **device manufacturer's own** production and quality-management systems — its scope section says plainly that it does not cover "device software functions," software that itself meets the legal definition of a medical device. BECS is a device. It's out of scope for that guidance entirely, on both sides of this question: not because of what the guidance says, but because of what it was never written to reach. Second, even where that guidance does apply, it's FDA guidance, not regulation — it describes a risk-based approach to testing rigor, not a replacement for the validation obligation 211.68(a) itself sets. Neither fact lets Lakeshore drop scripted testing on BECS.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your sysadmin's position — "it's a Category 4 vendor product, the vendor tested it, we run a smoke test" — would he be right if VAL-1203's risk assessment specifically concluded every affected function was low-risk?

If that conclusion were actually documented and reasoned — not just assumed from the category label — then a lighter test plan for those specific functions could be defensible. The problem with his actual position isn't that light testing is always wrong; it's that he's reasoning from the category instead of from a risk assessment. "Category 4" alone never answers the question. A dated, signed risk assessment that says why a function is low-risk, consistent with FDA's guidance that most software hazards should be assumed likely rather than unlikely unless shown otherwise, is what would actually justify a lighter touch — and that assessment has to exist and say so in writing, not live in his head.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Which GAMP category does the LIS-to-BECS translation script fall into, and what does that imply for how VAL-1203 should test it?

Category 5 — custom, bespoke code, because Lakeshore itself built and maintains it. That's the category with the least outside scrutiny already behind it: no vendor built it, no vendor tested it, no vendor support contract backs it. It implies the opposite of a smoke test — it needs its own full URS-to-PQ treatment, written and tested as thoroughly as any Category 4 critical function, because nobody else has ever validated a single line of it. A draft URS with no row for it at all isn't a gap to note later. It's a component that hasn't started being validated.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now have the vocabulary and the logic: categories sort software, a documented risk
assessment sets how hard to test it, and the V-model is the shape connecting every requirement to
the test that answers it. What you don't have yet is what that testing actually looks like once
it's executed — what IQ, OQ, and PQ evidence has to contain, how a traceability matrix proves
every requirement was actually tested, and how to tell a test that could fail from one that never
really tried. That's `iq-oq-pq-and-traceability`, next, where VAL-1203's full executed package
lands on your desk.
